...among the ancients. For Plato thinks that vision occurs through a shared brilliance, namely the light flowing out from the eyes to the surrounding air, meeting the light reflected back from bodies. He suggests that the light in the middle air easily flows into and joins with the fire-like power of sight, which is capable of expansion and transformation. Galen <note>An influential Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> agrees with Plato on this point. However, Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note> says that rays extended from the eyes as far as those bodies, touching them as if with a kind of palpitation, return the perception of them to the sight. 

The Epicureans <note>Followers of the philosophy of Epicurus</note>, on the other hand, affirm that <term>simulacra</term> <gloss>images or likenesses</gloss> of things that appear actually force themselves into the eyes. Aristotle, however, believes that these images are not physical bodies, but that they reach the sight from visible things through a change in the quality of the surrounding air. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher</note> maintains that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing; instead, he believes the soul itself, recognizing itself as visible—and being the one soul shared by all things—recognizes itself in everything that exists. 

Furthermore, Geometers and experts in optics, following Hipparchus in a certain way, describe certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays which are emitted through the eyes. From this, they believe the sight grasps many visible things at once, but those things are seen most clearly wherever the rays coincide. But indeed, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; a prominent Arab philosopher and scientist known for his work on optics</note> teaches something entirely different regarding aspects. Truly, it seems to Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian</note> that the power of the soul effects something in the eye that has not yet been fully investigated by those devoted to wisdom. 

Therefore, this science contributes greatly to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of the celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions. It also serves architecture in the measurement of buildings. Most closely, however, it provides a great deal of ornament to the art of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, such that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it demonstrates by what method we may avoid creating disproportionate or deformed figures in images that are viewed, accounting for distances and heights.

<summary>Agrippa catalogues various classical and medieval theories on the mechanism of sight before discussing the practical applications of optics in astronomy, architecture, and painting.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Galen, Hipparchus, Epicureans, Aristotle, Porphyry, Al-Kindi, Augustine, optics, vision, light rays, perspective, art theory</keywords>
